big: Fixed deposits feel dull and equity feels scary. Hybrid funds sit in the middle, but "hybrid" is a family of very different funds, not one product.

lines: I want something between an FD and equity. What are my options?
There are several middle paths, and they are not the same. First see what each one must hold, then how each behaved in a bad patch.

alt: Bars showing the equity, debt and gold shares that conservative, aggressive and multi asset hybrids must keep, and a dial for balanced advantage
caps: A conservative hybrid keeps only 10% to 25% in equity. The rest is mostly debt.
An aggressive hybrid holds 65% to 80% in equity, so it behaves much like an equity fund.
A multi asset fund must hold at least three asset classes, with at least 10% in each.
A balanced advantage fund has no fixed split. A model moves its equity up and down with valuations.
The category name tells you the rough mix. That mix decides how big the falls can be.

alt: Three lines for a conservative hybrid, an aggressive hybrid and an equity fund over ten years with the deepest fall of each marked
caps: Made-up paths, same ten years. Equity fund, aggressive hybrid (70% equity), conservative hybrid (15% equity).
In year 4 equity falls hard. The debt part of each hybrid softens the blow.
Deepest falls: equity -28%, aggressive hybrid -19%, conservative hybrid -3%.
A smaller fall usually comes with a smaller end value. Hybrids trade growth for a smoother ride.

intro: Rough mix, in a line each. Always read the factsheet for the live numbers.
rows: Hedged equity, steady like low-risk debt
3 or more classes, 10% each at least
note: The two paths above are made up. Real funds in a category can differ in how they use their range.

q: A factsheet shows a fund with 50% in equity, 30% in debt and 20% in gold. Meena asks which category it is and why it is not an aggressive hybrid. What is the right answer?
opts: Balanced advantage, since a fund with equity near half is always called dynamic
Conservative hybrid, since debt and gold together form a large share
Multi asset, since it holds three asset classes with at least 10% in each
Aggressive hybrid, since it holds more than one asset class together
why: Balanced advantage is defined by a model that moves equity with valuations, not by sitting near half equity.
Conservative hybrid keeps equity at only 10% to 25%. Here equity is 50%, so it falls outside that range.
Three classes, each at 10% or more, is the multi asset test. Aggressive needs 65% to 80% equity, which this lacks.
Holding several classes is not enough. An aggressive hybrid needs 65% to 80% in equity, and this fund has 50%.

q: Meena says she will panic if ₹1 lakh ever shows less than ₹90,000. In a bad stretch like the film, only one holding keeps her above that line. Which one?
opts: Conservative hybrid, which fell only about 3%, to roughly ₹97,000
Aggressive hybrid, whose debt part protects it against any real fall
Equity fund, since it rebounds fastest once the fall is over
Any hybrid, since every hybrid holds some debt to cushion falls
why: A 15% equity share fell only about 3% in the film. ₹1 lakh would show about ₹97,000, inside her limit.
With 70% in equity the film's aggressive hybrid fell about 19%. ₹1 lakh would show nearly ₹81,000.
The equity fund fell about 28% and left ₹72,000 on paper. A quick rebound does not stop the panic before it.
Hybrids differ widely. A 70% equity hybrid can fall nearly as far as equity, so having some debt is not enough.

q: A client says: "A hybrid gives FD-like safety with equity-like growth, so I will put my emergency money in it." What is the honest reply?
opts: Hybrids are safe, as the debt part is guaranteed by the fund house
Only aggressive hybrids fall, so a conservative one is as safe as an FD
Hybrids never fall by more than 10% because of the rules set by SEBI
A hybrid can fall, and how far depends on how much equity it holds
why: No guarantee exists. Debt can fall in value when rates rise and can default, so the debt part carries risk too.
A conservative hybrid falls less, but still holds equity and risky debt. It is not an FD and can show a loss.
No rule caps a fall at 10%. Category rules set the equity range, not the loss a fund may suffer.
It admits a hybrid can fall and ties the size of the fall to the equity share, which is the useful guide.

q: Rohan sees two funds both named "Balanced" and assumes they hold the same mix. Which check tells him what each really holds?
opts: The fund house, since one house runs all its funds the same way
The category and the actual equity share on each factsheet
The last one-year return, since it reveals the equity share
The size of each fund, since bigger funds hold more equity
why: One house runs many funds with different mandates. The house name does not fix a fund's equity share.
The category sets the allowed range and the factsheet shows the live mix. A name alone proves nothing.
A one-year return reflects the market that year. It does not reveal what the fund actually holds.
Fund size says how much money is in the fund, not how it is split between equity and debt.

pts: Hybrid is a family. The category tells you the rough equity share.
More equity means a bigger possible fall and more growth.
Read the factsheet mix, not the fund's name.
